title: Rare trait, common gene copy
hook: Only 1 in 10,000 shows a recessive trait. How common is the gene copy behind it?

knows: people carry two copies of each gene, one from each parent
a recessive trait shows only with two copies
doesNotKnow: that the share showing a recessive trait is the allele share squared (Hardy-Weinberg)
that most copies of a rare recessive allele sit in carriers who look normal

misconception: If a recessive trait is rare, almost nobody has the allele.
objective: The learner can explain that at 1 in 10,000 affected the allele share is 1 in 100, so about 2 x 1/100 = 1 in 50 people carry one copy, about 198 carriers for each affected person.

claims.text: Under Hardy-Weinberg conditions, the share with two copies of an allele is q^2 and the share with exactly one copy is 2pq, where q is the allele's share of all copies and p = 1 - q.
claims.source: Hartl D.L. & Clark A.G. (2007) Principles of Population Genetics, 4th ed., ch. 2.

claims.text: If 1 in 10,000 show the trait, the variant is 1 copy in 100 (q = 0.01) and carriers = 2 x 0.99 x 0.01 = 0.0198: 198 of 10,000, about 1 in 50, which is 198 carriers per person showing the trait.
On the stage: at 1 in 2,500, 4 affected and 392 carriers; at 1 in 400, 25 and 950; at 1 in 100, 100 affected and 1,800 carriers (18 per affected person).
claims.source: Same formula: q = 0.02, 0.05, 0.1; 2pq x 10,000 = 392, 950, 1,800. Counts are expected values, not a random draw.

claims.text: The model assumes random mating, no selection, migration or new mutations, and a large population; the trait and town are made up.
claims.source: Hardy-Weinberg conditions (Hartl & Clark 2007 ch. 2). Positions of people in the town are shuffled with an untuned seed (mulberry32(7)); they carry no information.

claims.text: With the variant at 1 copy in 100, two copies together occur 1 in 100 x 1 in 100 = 1 in 10,000 times (copies combine independently), so two copies are rare while one copy is not; the stage shows the same product for 1 in 2,500 (50 x 50), 1 in 400 (20 x 20) and 1 in 100 (10 x 10).
claims.source: q^2 = 0.0001 with q = 0.01; 1/q = 100, 50, 20, 10 for the four settings (same formula as c1).

recall.question: A made-up recessive trait shows in 1 in 40,000 people (random mating). Roughly how do carriers compare with people who show it?
recall.why: q = 1/200, so carriers are about 2/200 = 1 in 100, which is 400 times 1 in 40,000. The rarer the trait, the more copies hide in carriers.
